source.title: AI Safety at the Frontier: Paper Highlights, April '25

page_placements.theme: Scalable-oversight games: Guard and Houdini Elo against general capability, and nested oversight success

record.tranche_reason: The post discusses scalable oversight, but summarizes game-based oversight results rather than testing weak-label fine-tuning or performance gap recovered.
record.gate_note: The weak-to-strong section summarizes Scaling Laws For Scalable Oversight. Its game-based Elo slopes and Nested Scalable Oversight success rates are related to oversight scalability, but do not measure the weak-to-strong fine-tuning behavior or PGR in any claim version. These related results are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: A newsletter post that summarizes Scaling Laws For Scalable Oversight. That work models oversight as Guard/Houdini games with Elo scaling. No strong model is fine-tuned on weak labels and no PGR is reported, so no version is tested. The post loosely equates weak-to-strong generalization with scalable oversight, but the summarized results concern game win rates, not weak-label fine-tuning.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The post calls the NSO results discouraging: success is below 52% at 400 Elo gaps and declines further at larger gaps. It also notes limitations: single-step games, the poorly fitting Double ReLU model, and prompting rather than fine-tuning to induce adversarial behavior.
record.recipe_differences: The summarized work evaluates game-based Guard/Houdini oversight and recursive NSO; it does not fine-tune a strong model on a weak model's labels or measure PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling relationships differ by game; NSO success also varies by game and declines at larger Elo gaps.

fits_no_version.finding: Guard slopes range from nearly flat (Backdoor Code) to positive (Debate); Houdini slopes vary oppositely.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Oversight-game performance of the weaker overseer scales with general capability differently by game.

fits_no_version.finding: NSO success at 400 Elo gaps ranges from 9.8% (Wargames) to 51.4% (Debate), declining at larger gaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Nested game-based oversight success is low and falls as the capability gap grows.

record.problems: The post reports that the oversight games are simplified single-step interactions, the Double ReLU model is ad hoc and fits poorly for many games (R² as low as 0.0136 for Debate Houdinis), and prompting rather than fine-tuning to induce adversarial behavior may underestimate deceptive capabilities. No uncertainty estimates are given in the summary.
record.rows_left_out: The summary also mentions overall NSO results for all four games and the toy Counting-to-21 validation, but provides no per-game success rates beyond Wargames and Debate and no specific result needed to assess the weak-label fine-tuning claim.

untested.parts: No training methods for weak-to-strong fine-tuning.
No PGR by size, task or representation; the Elo scaling is for oversight games, not PGR.
No weak-to-strong failure modes measured; NSO decline at larger gaps concerns game-based oversight.
The Double ReLU/NSO modelling is about oversight game success, not conditions for a student to beat its supervisor.

record.verdict_notes: This is a secondary summary (newsletter), not primary research. The rows are properly linked to none.

versions.untested_parts: No strong student is fine-tuned on weak-model labels; no comparison with a weak supervisor or PGR is reported.
No auxiliary confidence loss, supervisor ensembling, or loss variant for weak-to-strong fine-tuning is tested.
No PGR comparisons across model sizes, NLP, chess, reward modelling, or representations are reported.
No weak-to-strong fine-tuning failure modes or distribution-shift effects are tested.
No theoretical conditions for a student trained on weak labels to beat its supervisor are given.
